title: Prayer, the church's banquet
hookLine: George Herbert's poem Prayer (I): a string of images for prayer
tomorrow: what could turn sweeping a dusty floor into gold?

cards: Thanksgiving table. Somebody says, would you pray? And every face turns your way.
In that second there are two roads. Reach for words someone else wrote, the ones the whole table half knows. Or make it up, out loud, from scratch.
Christians argue, gently, about which is better. George Herbert wrote a poem called Prayer, and how many ways does it say what prayer is? It never stops to finish a sentence.

teach.b: It opens: "Prayer the church's banquet, angels' age, God's breath in man returning to his birth, The soul in paraphrase, heart in pilgrimage." Listen for the two sides of the table argument inside it.
One side says: pray in words the church hands you. Prayer is a banquet, a meal everyone eats together, from the same table.
And look at "the soul in paraphrase": your soul said in other words, sometimes better words than you'd find at a hospital bed at midnight. Written prayers carry you when you have nothing.
The other side says: pray from your own heart. And Herbert gives them lines too. "God's breath in man returning to his birth": breath going back to the one who breathed it in.
"Heart in pilgrimage": a heart on the road, with no script. Some churches lean on written prayers read together; some lean on prayers made up on the spot.
He piles up image after image, "Heaven in ordinary, man well drest," and then lands, with the shortest name of all: "The land of spices; something understood." Not well said. Understood.
Whichever road you take at the table, the poem says the point is on the other end.

how: Some Christians pray mostly in set words, such as the Lord's Prayer or a prayer book's collects, often said together; others pray mostly in their own words, aloud or silently; many churches use both.

o: a church meal served after the Sunday morning service
a list of requests read aloud by a minister each week
talking with God: in Herbert's poem, finally being understood

games.q: Herbert's names for prayer — tap the pairs.
p: your soul said in other words

s: Herbert's poem defines prayer in one tidy sentence
it never finishes a sentence: it piles up names, a banquet, a breath, a pilgrimage, and ends on something understood.
the poem gives images that fit both written prayers and made-up ones
the church's banquet and the soul in paraphrase, beside a heart in pilgrimage.
a prayer only counts if you make up the words yourself
Christians pray both ways. Herbert's soul in paraphrase is a soul said in other words.

games.q: your friend only prays in her own words and says written prayers feel fake. she asks you for the best case for the written kind. what do you say?
o: when you have no words, they lend you some: the soul in paraphrase.
older words are holier, so God pays more attention to them.
they stop you from ever saying something wrong in front of people.
games.why: the best case is Herbert's: a banquet shared at one table, and words that say your soul when you can't. her side's best case is in the poem too: a heart in pilgrimage.

practice: On a scrap of paper, by hand, write one image of your own for prayer, the way Herbert did: two or three words, a thing you can see. A porch light. A text left on read.
Then sit with your image and Herbert's last two words, something understood, side by side.

wordCard.voice: Prayer. In Herbert's poem, a banquet, a breath going home, a heart on the road, and at the very end, something understood.

carryVoice: Your line: something understood. Written or made up, Herbert lands on what happens at the other end. Until tomorrow.
